original_question: Let f : P^N -> P^N be a morphism of degree d >= 2 defined over Q, and assume that for every 1 <= n <= N + 1 the first coordinate function of f^n is not a constant multiple of X_0^(d^n). Then every wandering point P in P^N(Q) has only finitely many forward-orbit points that are integral relative to the hyperplane X_0 = 0; equivalently, if f^n(P) = [A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)] in primitive integral coordinates, then log|A_0(n)| / log max(|A_0(n)|, ..., |A_N(n)|) tends to 1 as n -> infinity.
target_in_paper: Section 21, Conjecture 21.4 (Dynamical Lang-Siegel Conjecture for P^N), together with the immediately preceding definition of integrality relative to the hyperplane x_0 = 0, and the nearby motivating context from Proposition 21.1, Theorem 21.2, Theorem 21.3, and Remark 21.5.
correct_elements: Your draft clearly aims at the paper's higher-dimensional integral-points problem on projective space. It correctly matches the ambient space P^N, the field Q, the degree condition d >= 2, the iterate-wise hypothesis on the first coordinate of f^n for 1 <= n <= N+1, the hyperplane x_0 = 0, and the sharpened coordinate-growth conclusion involving primitive integral coordinates [A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)]. These are the distinctive ingredients of Conjecture 21.4.
missing_details: The paper states this as a conjecture/open problem, not as a proved theorem.
The official formulation first quantifies over every P in P^N(Q); the extra assumption that P is wandering appears only in the stronger second clause.

The phrase 'integral relative to the hyperplane x_0 = 0' must be defined explicitly: P in P^N(Q) is integral relative to x_0 = 0 if it has homogeneous coordinates [1, a_1, ..., a_N] with a_1, ..., a_N in Z.

To make 'the first coordinate function of f^n' stand-alone, one should specify that if f^n = [F_0^(n):...:F_N^(n)] is written by homogeneous polynomials of degree d^n with no common factor, then the hypothesis is F_0^(n) != c X_0^(d^n) for every nonzero constant c and every 1 <= n <= N+1.
The orbit notation O_f(P) = {f^n(P) : n >= 0} should be made explicit.
The definition of 'wandering' should be supplied: O_f(P) is infinite.
In the stronger clause, one should specify 'for each n >= 1' and that f^n(P) = [A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)] is written in primitive integral coordinates with gcd(A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)) = 1.
The paper does not present the limit statement as equivalent to the finiteness statement; it introduces it as a stronger 'More precisely' refinement.
Remark 21.5 notes that number fields and S-integers are possible generalizations, but the official statement in this paper is over Q only.
No nilpotency condition appears anywhere in this statement, so none should be added.
refined_question: Conjecture 21.4 (Dynamical Lang-Siegel Conjecture for P^N): Let f = [f_0, ..., f_N] : P^N -> P^N be a morphism of degree d >= 2 defined over Q. For each 1 <= n <= N+1, write the iterate f^n = [F_0^(n) : ... : F_N^(n)] by homogeneous polynomials of degree d^n with no common factor, and assume that F_0^(n) is not a constant multiple of X_0^(d^n). If O_f(P) = {f^n(P) : n >= 0} is the forward orbit of P in P^N(Q), must O_f(P) contain only finitely many points that are integral relative to the hyperplane x_0 = 0, i.e. points admitting homogeneous coordinates [1, a_1, ..., a_N] with a_1, ..., a_N in Z? More precisely, if P is wandering and for each n >= 1 one writes f^n(P) = [A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)] in primitive integral coordinates with gcd(A_0(n), ..., A_N(n)) = 1, must lim_{n->infty} log|A_0(n)| / log max{|A_0(n)|, ..., |A_N(n)|} = 1?
justification: The draft is trying to capture the survey's higher-dimensional dynamical analogue of Lang-Siegel, namely Conjecture 21.4 in Section 21. The surrounding context confirms this: Proposition 21.1 gives the one-variable geometric obstruction behind the iterate hypothesis, Theorem 21.2 is the basic finiteness result for integers in one-dimensional orbits, and Theorem 21.3 is the stronger P^1 asymptotic statement that motivates the 'More precisely' clause in Conjecture 21.4. Your draft preserves most of the paper's technical content, but it is not fully paper-faithful because it turns a conjecture into a theorem, restricts the primary finiteness claim to wandering points even though the paper states that clause for all rational points, and treats the asymptotic clause as equivalent when the paper presents it only as a stronger refinement.
